To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the occlusal anatomy and margin design significantly affected the margin strength of ceramic inlay/onlay restorations and that e.maxTM porcelain was significantly stronger than EmpressTM porcelain at the margin.
the thicker margins (45°angles) are stronger than the thinner ones (60° angles) for both IPS EmpressTM (n=10) and IPS e.max® (n=10).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fracture strength of the margin between an IPS EmpressTM or e.maxTM inlay and the tooth.
the fracture of ceramic inlays at the margins, where the porcelain is thin and is subjected to stress from the tooth.
the strength of the margins of ceramic inlays.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fracture strength of ceramic inlays is affected by the margin angle and porcelain material.
the occlusal anatomy and margin design are critical factors that affect the fracture resistance of ceramic restorations, and that the porcelain material is a critical variable.
• The occlusal margin fracture strength of ceramic inlays is influenced by the porcelain material, the occlusal anatomy of the cavity preparation, the margin angle and the margin location.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
for both e.max™ and Empress™, the 45° angled margins were significantly (p<0.05) stronger than the 6°0 margins.
for both e.max and Empress, the 45 degrees angles are significantly stronger than the margins with 60 degrees.

the occlusal anatomy (cusp height), margin design (thickness) and porcelain material are all critical factors that significantly influence the margin strength of ceramic restorations [36,39-41,43-46].
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single design or material that can be recommended for all clinical situations.
there are several factors that can affect the fracture strength of ceramic inlays and onlays.

occlusal anatomy and margin design are critical factors that can significantly affect the strength of ceramic inlay/onlay restorations, and that the occlusal margin should be designed to be at least 2mm in thickness to minimize stress concentration and to provide a margin that will not fail prematurely.
